The [case study](../../cases/eu-frames/index.qmd), which presents the original paper, the Multi100 project and the five reanalyses on which every track of the case is built, is the place to start.

This version of the one-day course on the EU-frames case keeps the statistical methods in the foreground, and its centre is the robustness of a published claim. The claim is that of the original author (OA) of a paper about how citizens of the member states frame the European Union, which five analysts reanalysed for the Multi100 project. You write the estimand behind the claim and finish a causal graph for it. You reproduce, to the third decimal, the result that Multi100 recorded for one of the three analysts whose analyses rest on means of countries or of cells, chosen by you, and the three reproduced models lead into the methods that a panel of 27 countries needs: fixed effects and random intercepts, the within–between model, and the CR2 test for few clusters. Then the specification menu is taken apart decision by decision, you explore it and put an exploratory dot on the live class chart, and you declare one analysis in a shortened preregistration before you run it and submit it as a declared dot. The chart is read against the curve of 864 specifications of the claim.

The day works on aggregate data only, the country-year panel of the course and two files that the course rebuilt for two of the analysts; the analyses of respondents belong to the three-day course. It is taught in the [browser lab](../../cases/eu-frames/lab.qmd), which runs R inside a web page with the data in place, so nothing needs to be installed, and the downloadable workspace is the option for those who have installed R and an IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.). The day assumes that a linear model and its output are not new to you. It runs as four parts of ninety minutes, with breaks of thirty, sixty and thirty minutes between them, and several of its steps are things that the class does together, so it needs a facilitator.

| | What happens | Length |
|---|---|---|
| [Before the day](before.qmd) | Open the browser lab once, read the case study and fit one model; installing R and an IDE is optional. | 1 to 3 hours |
| [Part 1 – The case and the vocabulary](part-1.qmd) | The credibility debate, what 'replication' names, and the five analysts of the claim; then the browser lab runs on every machine. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 2 – The estimand and the causal graph](part-2.qmd) | The paper in full, estimands and the causal-graph crash course; you write the estimand and finish the graph. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 3 – Reproduction and the specification menu](part-3.qmd) | You reproduce the result of C6HJR, KQXUE or 018OL, read the three models side by side, meet the problem of few clusters, and work the menu, ending with an exploratory dot on the class chart. | 90 minutes |
| [Part 4 – Multiverse and preregistration](part-4.qmd) | The class chart against the curve of the claim, what the curve establishes and what it cannot, and the analysis that you preregister before it runs. | 90 minutes |
| [After the day](after.qmd) | Every model of the menu output by output, and the rest of the methods strand. | as you like |

The other two one-day formats on this case put [open science](../eu-frames-one-day-open-science/index.qmd) or the [data tools](../eu-frames-one-day-data-tools/index.qmd) in the foreground, and the [three-day course](../eu-frames-three-days/index.qmd) builds the data from the raw survey files and reproduces all five analysts.
